title: [2511.18303] Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery

sections.heading: Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery

content.text: We present a long-horizon, hierarchical deep research (DR) agent designed for complex materials and device discovery problems that exceed the scope of existing Machine Learning (ML) surrogates and closed-source commercial agents. Our framework instantiates a locally deployable DR instance that integrates local retrieval-augmented generation with large language model reasoners, enhanced by a Deep Tree of Research (DToR) mechanism that adaptively expands and prunes research branches to maximize coverage, depth, and coherence. We systematically evaluate across 27 nanomaterials/device topics using a large language model (LLM)-as-judge rubric with five web-enabled state-of-the-art models as jurors. In addition, we conduct dry-lab validations on five representative tasks, where human experts use domain simulations (e.g., density functional theory, DFT) to verify whether DR-agent proposals are actionable. Results show that our DR agent produces reports with quality comparable to— and often exceeding— those of commercial systems (ChatGPT-5-thinking/o3/o4-mini-high Deep Research) at a substantially lower cost, while enabling on-prem integration with local data and tools.
Keywords: deep research, hierarchical reasoning, materials discovery, retrieval-augmented generation, large language models, computational materials science, autonomous agents

Machine learning (ML) for nanomaterials and device discovery has advanced from tractable single-entity predictions to increasingly complex, system-level challenges. At the molecular or crystal level (S1), modern surrogates routinely predict intrinsic properties [xie2018cgcnn]. Small assemblies (S2)—interfaces, heterostructures, or simple 2–3-component devices—introduce coupling effects yet remain manageable. Real-world nano-devices, however, operate at system scope (S3): multi-layer perovskite stacks with interdependent layers, core–shell–doped catalysts with engineered interfaces, or nano-architected battery electrodes where transport across length scales governs performance [severson2019cyclelife]. The ultimate challenge lies in cross-domain integration (S4): platforms that span material families, recognition chemistries, and transduction modalities—for example, engineering 2D-material field-effect transistor (FET) sensors with aptamer functionalization for environmental detection [szymanski2023alab, wang2022aptamer\_gfet].

Meeting this escalation in scope requires a matching escalation in depth. We frame depth from single-pass prediction/forward screening (D1), to multi-stage pipelines with structured outputs (D2), to long-horizon synthesis with iterative planning (D3), and ultimately hierarchical, breadth–depth exploration (D4). While recent agentic frameworks have successfully demonstrated hierarchical orchestration for complex scientific workflows [gottweis2025towards, ghafarollahi2025sciagents, zou2025elagente], ensuring robust execution and simulation management, device/system-level optimization and design (S3–S4) presents a distinct challenge. The governing laws for device integration are not fully encoded in standard simulation packages, requiring long-horizon hierarchical autonomous discovery (D3–D4) with potential to navigate the combinatorial explosion of processing parameters sparsely distributed across heterogeneous knowledge sources. Existing approaches typically face limitations in this unstructured knowledge regime [montoya2020camd, merchant2023gnome, chanussot2021oc20, levine2025omol25] (Detailed in Appendix [A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A1 "Appendix A Related Work in Physics ML Surrogates, Domain LLMs, and Agentic Systems ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")).

To address this gap, we introduce a hierarchical deep-research (DR) agent111We use *Deep Research (DR)* to denote a single-threaded, iterative retrieval–reasoning–writing loop run by one agent. *Deep Tree of Research (DToR)* denotes a tree-structured orchestration that spawns and selects among multiple DR branches with hierarchical planning and merge. Throughout, ”hierarchical deep research” is synonymous with DToR; we henceforth use only DR and DToR for clarity. purpose-built for long-horizon scientific inquiry. Given a natural-language inquiry, the system instantiates a locally deployable DR instance that iterates between local and web retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and large language model (LLM) reasoners (summarizers, reflectors). We further expand the DR instance into a Deep Tree of Research (DToR) where each instance is treated as a node in a tree-structured workflow. DToR adaptively expands/prunes branches to improve coverage, depth, and coherence. The agent is self-directed/navigated (plans its own research path), runs locally for controllability and privacy, and targets S3–S4 hypotheses. At a glance, our goal is to measure synthesis quality by a programmatic evaluation harness (anchored rubric, A/B preferences) plus dry-lab checks. We then show that orchestration via DToR consistently improves synthesis quality over single-instance DR across model backbones and local-corpus budgets at comparable compute.

Contributions. (1) A democratized, locally deployable framework for scientific deep research, enabling materials researchers to exercise fine-grained control over cost and preferences using open-source LLMs while achieving performance that surpasses commercial state-of-the-art solutions in most cases (§[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S3 "3 Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). (2) A hierarchical orchestration (DToR) that yields robust gains over single-instance DR across LLM backbones and local data budgets, supported by comprehensive factorial and targeted component ablations. (3) An evaluation program combining anchored rubric scores, repeated A/B duels, and dry-lab validation to assess synthesis quality.

Recent work on structured reasoning for LLMs has moved beyond linear prompting toward explicit search structures. Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) frames inference as a branching search over intermediate ‘thoughts’, while Graph-of-Thoughts (GoT) generalizes this to arbitrary graphs to model non-linear dependencies and subproblem coordination [yao2023tree, besta2024graph, yao2024effectivegot]. In parallel, reason–act and self-improvement paradigms—ReAct, Reflexion, and Self-Refine—provide strong baselines for multi-step decision-making and revision ([yao2022react, shinn2023reflexion, madaan2023selfrefine]). Foundational web-agent environments/benchmarks—BrowseComp, WebLINX, WebArena, and BrowserGym—formalize browsing/navigation competencies and support reproducible evaluation [wei2025browsecomp, pan2024weblinx, zhou2023webarena, lesellier2024browsergym]. Work on retrieval is also moving toward more adaptive strategies: Self-RAG [asai2024selfrag] learns when to retrieve and critique outputs, CRAG [yan2024crag] evaluates retrieval quality and escalates to web search when evidence is weak, and GraphRAG [peng2024graphragsurvey] uses graph-structured knowledge for non-flat retrieval. Despite this progress, there is no framework that unifies structured branching and adaptive retrieval in a way that scales under practical compute and data limits for domain-specific research settings.

D4 requires structured and budget-aware planning beyond short-term queries. We introduce DToR, a breadth-then-depth controller for DR that starts from multiple parallel perspectives, selectively expands or prunes based on explicit gap checks, runs evidence-first research steps (local RAG with adapted web search), and produces source-grounded reports.

As shown in Fig. [S1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F1 "Figure S1 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")222Supporting figures (S1–S13) illustrating detailed experimental results and supplementary analyses are presented in Appendix [B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2 "Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"). (with comparison against common standard DR agent [langchain2025localdeepresearcher]), each DR instance is an evidence-first loop that (1) generates a search query; (2) performs local RAG; (3) summarizes local evidence; (4) generates a complementary query to induce topical diversity; (5) conducts web research for both queries; (6) integrates/updates previous retrieved segments in a running summary; (7) reflects to propose follow-up query. The process would loop until a set maximum round before (8) finalizing. Three design choices distinguish this instance from common local DR agents[langchain2025localdeepresearcher] which only conduct (1)-(5)-(6)-(7): local-first retrieval (before web) to reduce drift, hallucination, and surface domain priors; diversity-aware query generation (local summary derived complementary query) to guarantee comprehensiveness; and robust I/O discipline to prevent controller stalls on local-hosted LLMs. Compared with classic ReAct/Reflexion-style linear loops, this instance adds an explicit breadth mechanism and escalation policy akin to adaptive/corrective-RAG, while remaining compatible with the drop-in alternative RAG methods.

children.heading: 2.2 DToR: from perspectives to gap-driven expansion

content.text: Based on the single DR instance, we treat each DR instance as a Research Node (RN) inside a branch-and-bound controller (Fig. [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Method ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). Starting from a user query, a diversifier proposes several orthogonal Perspectives (P1, P2…)—each seeds one branch with a budget: maximum depth, nodes per branch, and total branches. For the active branch, the router (i) runs the next pending RN (the single DR instance), producing a RN summary; (ii) invokes analyst based on remaining depth/budget/current RN report quality to give a decision EXPAND, PRUNE; and, if EXPAND with budget remaining, (iii) invokes knowledge gap explorer to materializes new RNs from this RN targeted to those gaps (depth+1) and updates remaining budget. Branches that stagnate are pruned; (iv) branches that reach depth or converge are synthesized into a perspective report. When all branches reach synthesis, a final synthesizer reconciles cross-branch evidence, resolves conflicts, and outputs a provenance-rich, consolidated report. Conceptually, this is a tree-of-search over (query, evidence, summary) states rather than over purely symbolic "thoughts," inheriting the benefits of structured exploration/backtracking from tree/graph-based reasoning while remaining tailored to information-seeking and citation fidelity under explicit resource budgets.

We evaluate across 27 expert-crafted topics spanning materials and devices (e.g., per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) FET probes, CO2 sensing in 2D materials, Li/Na-selective membranes, CO2-reduction catalysts); full topic prompts are provided in Appendix [C](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A3 "Appendix C Nanomaterials and Device Topics ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"). For each topic, we consider 41 agents—11 commercial and 30 local (split evenly between single DR-instance and DToR-mode)—on consumer-level hardware. We evaluate local agents across LLM backbones (gpt-oss120B, gpt-oss20B, QwQ32B) and local RAG budgets (local0/local100/local500), holding orchestration fixed and varying only backbone and corpus size; full agent configurations in Appendix [D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A4 "Appendix D Local DR Experimental Settings ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"). Using an LLM-as-judge protocol (Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5 "Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")), we generate 41 distinct report variants per topic and have five web-enabled SOTA judges—Claude 4 Opus (thinking), Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok-3 (thinking), ChatGPT-o3, and ChatGPT-o4-mini-high—score each report under a fixed, double-blind rubric (judges are blinded to agent identities) with five equally weighted dimensions—(1) relevance, (2) depth, (3) clarity, (4) applicability, and (5) novelty—whose concise definitions are provided in Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5 "Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery").

Judge view and anonymization: LLM judges see only the final report text—no agent/model identifiers, tool logs, or token/count metadata—and assign numeric scores on five anchored dimensions (relevance, depth/rigor, clarity/reproducibility, applicability, novelty) under a fixed instruction to “act as an experienced materials scientist” (Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5 "Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). The rubric provides positive/negative exemplars per dimension; unresolved contradictions or failure to reconcile conflicts between local and web evidence are penalized under Depth/Rigor and Clarity/Reproducibility, while reports that explicitly compare sources and justify a resolution are rewarded. Access to local vs. web contexts is controlled at generation time (agents run in local-only or web-enabled modes), whereas judges never see those contexts—only the synthesized report—so the evaluation targets synthesis/reasoning quality rather than retrieval exposure. Judges assign 0–10 per dimension with one-sentence justifications; numeric ratings are extracted by a deterministic parser. We repeat the evaluation three times per topic–report–judge combination, yielding 27×41×5×3=16,60527\times 41\times 5\times 3=16,605 rubric-based judgments. Inter-judge agreement (Pearson correlation on scores and Spearman rank correlation) remains high across all dimensions.

We then run A/B dueling preferences using the same setup. For each topic, we form three pools: commercial, local gpt-oss, and local non-gpt-oss. Within each pool we rank reports by rubric average and select the top-3; the resulting 9 reports then enter all pairwise duels ((92)=36\binom{9}{2}=36 pairs per topic). Duels are double-blind and order-randomized, guided by a concise “experienced materials scientist” prompt emphasizing clarity, gap prioritization, and actionable next steps. Each duel is repeated three times, yielding 27×36×3=2916​A/B27\times 36\times 3=2916A/B trials and 14,58014,580 individual judge decisions.

Finally, we conduct dry-lab validation on five representative tasks—PFAS sensor probe, PFAS degradation catalysts, battery binder selection, oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalyst stability, and CO2 sensor probe—by sending anonymized best-local and best-commercial reports to domain experts who extract candidates and build simulation environments (Appendix LABEL:app:dry\_lab\_details). We score ten simulation metrics per task with domain-standard protocols (e.g., explicit-solvent ab initio molecular dynamics, AIMD, when necessary) and aggregate per-task and overall performance; full simulation setups and metric definitions are in Appendix LABEL:app:dry\_lab\_details. We also run a full-factorial ablation across Method ×\times LLM backbone ×\times local-corpus budget (27 topics, 41 agents) to isolate main effects and interactions (Fig. [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Experimental results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")b), and conduct targeted component ablations on the best-performing configuration across three representative topics to further dissect orchestration contributions (Appendix LABEL:app:additional\_ablation). To characterize the benchmark itself, we compute per-topic difficulty (mean performance across agents) and discrimination power (standard deviation of agent scores), revealing which topics best separate strong from weak systems; full topic-level analysis is in Appendix LABEL:app:topic\_analysis. All runs were executed on a workstation with 4×\timesNVIDIA RTX A5500 (Ubuntu); completion-time statistics and energy estimates are reported in Appendix LABEL:app:power\_estimation. The DToR framework source code is publicly available at <https://github.com/ruiding-uchicago/DToR_deep_research>.

Across the five LLM-as-judge dimensions on 27 topics ×\times 41 agents (Fig. [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Experimental results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")a), DToR\_gpt-oss120B\_local500 (running DToR with gpt-oss120B and all 500 volumes of local corpus for RAG; see details in Appendix [D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A4 "Appendix D Local DR Experimental Settings ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")) achieves an average score of 8.57/10, ranking 1st overall. When the local RAG budget is reduced to local100 and local0, the scores remain 8.53/10 and 8.37/10, both still top-3. Even without the DToR controller (i.e., a single DR instance), gpt-oss120B reaches 8.33/10 (local100) and 8.32/10 (local500), ranking 4th and 5th. Under the same setup with gpt-oss20B, DToR yields 8.15/10, 8.12/10, and 8.08/10 for local500/local100/local0, respectively. All of the above surpass commercial baselines including ChatGPT-o4-mini-high (7.96/10), ChatGPT-o3 (7.95/10), and ChatGPT-5-thinking (7.85/10), as well as other widely used systems such as Gemini 2.5 Pro (7.81/10), Claude Opus 4 (7.78/10), Grok 3 (7.51/10), and Perplexity (7.51/10). Notably, DToR\_QwQ32B\_local500 driven by laptop compatible lightweight LLM also attains 7.80/10, outperforming roughly half of the commercial systems.

A closer look at the five dimensions (Fig. [S2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F2 "Figure S2 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")) shows that clarity and depth are the most challenging, with the lowest means and the largest dispersion. Even so, DToR yields the largest gains over a single-DR instance precisely on these two dimensions, with average improvements of +0.69 and +0.72, respectively. Excluding relevance—which exhibits a ceiling effect and thus limited separability—DToR delivers clear improvements on the remaining four dimensions. For example, on novelty and applicability, DToR improves Single\_gpt-oss120B\_local500 by +0.43 and +0.42 points on average, pushing it above the leading commercial baseline. Inter-rater consistency across the five LLM critics was high: average Pearson correlation p=0.97\mathrm{p}=0.97 on raw scores and Spearman ρ=0.97\rho=0.97 on rank orders (Fig. [S3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F3 "Figure S3 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")).

Reliability is further supported by agent-specific and inter-trial consistency (Fig. [S4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F4 "Figure S4 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"), Fig. [S5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F5 "Figure S5 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). From an ablation study perspective (Fig. [2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Experimental results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")b), enabling local RAG (7.21/10) and especially DToR mode (7.32/10) increases the average score. Across all 27 topics and 41 agents, Method ×\times Backbone ×\times Local-corpus budget factorial analysis shows that the dominant effect is orchestration: DToR consistently outperforms single-instance DR once a non-trivial local corpus is present (local100/local500), whereas at local0 the gap narrows and a strong backbone (gpt-oss120B) can close it. To further isolate orchestration components, we conducted targeted component ablations on the best-performing configuration (DToR\_gpt-oss120B\_local500) across three representative topics: systematically degrading tree depth (3→\rightarrow2 perspectives), reflection loops (3→\rightarrow0 iterations), and retrieval counts (5→\rightarrow1 papers per query) all reduce performance, with reflection proving most critical; removing web search (local-only or LLM-only modes) similarly degrades quality, confirming gap-triggered web complement adds value; driving the same orchestration with API models (gpt-5-mini/nano) maintains relative orderings but at materially higher cost (Fig. [S6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F6 "Figure S6 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"), Fig. [S7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F7 "Figure S7 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"), Fig. [S8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F8 "Figure S8 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"); full details in Appendix LABEL:app:additional\_ablation). Per-topic analysis reveals a clear difficulty spectrum: sensing/characterization tasks (in-situ TEM, printed FET arrays) are easiest, while battery electrochemistry topics (lithium ion battery: LIB binders, fluoroether anion receptors) are hardest; discrimination power shows environmental sensing topics (microplastics, antibiotics detection) separate agents weakly (σ≈0.7\sigma\approx 0.7), whereas battery/materials synthesis challenges (LIB fluoroether receptor, ambient-pressure diamond growth) sharply distinguish strong from weak systems (σ>1.1\sigma>1.1). Notably, topic difficulty and discrimination are decoupled: LIB\_Fluoroether\_Anion\_Receptor exhibits both the highest difficulty (μ=6.93\mu=6.93) and the largest discrimination (σ=1.24\sigma=1.24), sharply separating strong and weak agents; conversely, Microplastics\_Sensing\_2D shows the lowest discrimination (σ=0.69\sigma=0.69) at mid-pack difficulty (μ=7.19\mu=7.19); Catalytic\_Mineralization\_of\_Microplastics is relatively easy (μ=7.49\mu=7.49) yet still discriminates well (σ=1.03\sigma=1.03), while Wastewater\_Resource\_Recovery\_Cats is hard (μ=7.04\mu=7.04) but offers weak separation (σ=0.93\sigma=0.93). Critically, DToR agents maintain consistent performance advantages across both high-σ\sigma and low-σ\sigma topics, confirming that orchestration benefits are robust to topic characteristics rather than prompt-specific artifacts; full per-topic difficulty rankings and discrimination analysis are in Appendix LABEL:app:topic\_analysis.

To mitigate potential bias inherent in numerical rubric scoring, we further complement these results with pairwise dueling—a side-by-side comparison that directly elicits preferences from LLM judges without imposing a rigid numerical scale. Pairwise dueling (Fig. [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Experimental results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")) confirms these findings across all 27 topics (Fig. [S9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F9 "Figure S9 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")) with strong experimental consistency (Fig. [S10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F10 "Figure S10 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")): (1) DToR agents show a higher average win rate (58.6%) than Single DR agents (52.8%) in head-to-head comparisons; (2) DToR\_gpt-oss120B\_local500 achieves an impressive 79% mean win rate; (3) gpt-oss-driven DToR and Single agents both exhibit similarly high win rates above 74%, demonstrating a clear advantage. These outcomes further support the previous rubric scoring results, confirming that our locally hosted DToR agents generate superior DR reports.

In dry-lab validation spanning 10 metrics over five application scenarios (Fig. [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 Experimental results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")), we comprehensively validate across domain benchmarks with DFT and explicit-solvent AIMD, scoring each task against a well-recognized baseline normalized to 100. The tasks and metrics are: (i) PFAS sensor binding—static-DFT binding energies Δ​Ebind\Delta E\_{\text{bind}} for PFAS vs. interferents and explicit-solvent end-state potential-energy gaps from short AIMD, with selectivity scored as Δ​Δ​E\Delta\Delta E (PFAS minus interferent) and anchored to β\beta-cyclodextrin[wang2024reversible] (Score=100); (ii) PFAS degradation catalysis—C–F bond dissociation energies from constrained scans and solvated binding stability proxies, normalized to Ti4O7 (Magnéli)[lin2018ti4o7] as the domain benchmark (100); (iii) battery binder adhesion (on NCM811)—areal-normalized Δ​Ebind/A\Delta E\_{\text{bind}}/A (static DFT, contact area via convex-hull atoms within 3.5 Å) and explicit-solvent end-state gap (AIMD) to capture electrolyte competition, anchored to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF)[zhong2021pvdf] (100); (iv) OER catalyst stability—dissolution potential UdissU\_{\text{diss}} (tendency for surface metal leaching) and oxygen-vacancy formation energy VOV\_{\mathrm{O}} (lattice robustness), normalized to IrO2[ding2025oermulti] (100); and (v) CO2 sensor binding—grid-sampled static-DFT binding energies on candidate surfaces, linearly transformed and anchored to g-C3N4[karthik2023gc3n4co2] (100). Across these five applications, we observe four all-metrics >> 100 events (i.e., every metric for a task exceeds its baseline): commercial once on CO2 sensor; local DR (non-gpt-oss) twice on CO2 sensor and battery binder; and local DR (gpt-oss) once on PFAS degradation. In these cases, the DR-proposed candidates point to concrete, testable improvements over their domain baselines in terms of qualitative dry lab trials: for CO2 sensing, stronger and more uniform adsorption than g-C3N4 (reduced site-to-site dispersion); for battery binders, higher areal-normalized adhesion than PVDF under dry interfaces and competitive performance under explicit electrolyte; and for PFAS degradation, lower C–F dissociation energies relative to Ti4O7 while maintaining adequate adsorption stability. Notably, explicit-solvent AIMD often reorders static-DFT rankings, revealing candidates that look promising in vacuum but lose ground when solvation/competition is included—an effect we quantify in the AIMD score panels. The gpt-oss-based local DR agent leads on 7 out of 10 metrics when judged by per-metric averages and also achieves a higher overall score aggregating across metrics (98.7). Related details are available in Appendix LABEL:app:dry\_lab\_details.

While dry-lab simulations provide an initial filter, looking more closely at the candidates proposed by the DR agents reveals a feasibility gap in current LLM–RAG orchestration(Fig. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.2 Experimental results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). In PFAS sensing, the agents successfully identified rational designs like B1 and A1, yet DToR agent also produced “kitchen-sink” failures like C3, which stacks four mutually incompatible phases (hydrophobic fluorosilane, hydrophilic MXene, Ag nanoparticles, acidic PEDOT:PSS). In practice, synthesis of such a complex system would be infeasible, because the agents ignored likely colloidal incompatibilities (e.g., phase separation and acid-induced etching) that would render the device chemically unstable[cameron2020pedotpss, kumar2023mxenestability]. Similarly, for PFAS degradation, cost-effective and chemically robust candidates like C4 and A3 stand in contrast to C5, a triple heterostructure (MXene/g-C3N4/Al2O3) that neglects potential challenges in interfacial charge-transfer resistance and fabrication complexity[mandari2025gcn\_mxene\_review, bagnall2025al2o3\_stability]. These over-engineered failures stem from a fundamental limitation in current agent architectures: without intrinsic wet-lab feasibility priors, cost models, or external physics validators, LLMs are prone to “inverse-design hallucinations” [miret2025llms\_materials\_discovery, kalai2025hallucinate] that assume functional additivity where physical incompatibility exists. This underscores that future AI4Science frameworks must integrate dedicated domain-validator modules (e.g., synthesis-aware ReAct loops) to ground theoretical generation in experimental reality333Extended discussion with further citations is available in Appendix LABEL:candidate\_feasibility\_discussions..

All timings reflect a single-machine setup with serialized agent scheduling (energy estimation methodology in Appendix LABEL:app:power\_estimation); under this controlled setting, DToR with gpt-oss120B averages 19.6 h (Fig. [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 3.2 Experimental results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"), Fig. [S11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F11 "Figure S11 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). This should be viewed as an upper bound of orchestration cost, not a requirement for quality: a low-resource profile that disables local-corpus RAG finishes in <6<6 h (an overnight run), and a single-instance DR pipeline with gpt-oss120B typically completes within ∼\sim30 min—on the same order as commercial solutions yet, as shown earlier, with higher rubric and duel scores. Overall, our gains arise from orchestration and information coverage rather than “model pile-up”: users can explicitly tune for quality (DToR + corpus) or for cost/latency (DR/no-RAG) depending on resources. Without high subscription fees (Fig. [S12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F12 "Figure S12 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")) for commercial solutions, this framework offers flexible deployment from lightweight laptops to multi-node clusters444DToR branches can run in parallel; see <https://github.com/ruiding-uchicago/DToR_deep_research> for implementation details., enabling democratized, transparent, and open access to advanced research agents adaptable to diverse computational budgets of materials researchers.

We introduced DToR, a locally deployable DR agent with a resource-bounded tree controller that unifies local-first RAG, diversity-aware query generation, and gap-driven branching into provenance-rich, long-horizon information seeking. Across 27 topics and 41 agents, under 16,605 rubric judgments from 5 web-enabled judges, our best local model (DToR\_gpt-oss120B\_local500) ranked 1st (8.57/10) with a 79% mean duel win rate (14,580 dueling judgement) while using only 4.37 kWh/report on consumer devices. In dry-lab validation across five applications, its candidates matched or surpassed the best commercial solutions. This work highlights a practical path toward open, secure, and scalable on-prem DR agents for automated, accelerated scientific discovery at the S3–S4 level.

children.heading: Appendix A Related Work in Physics ML Surrogates, Domain LLMs, and Agentic Systems
A.1 Physics-aligned surrogates and classical ML

content.text: Physics-guided predictive surrogates now operate at web-scale, with graph networks and equivariant models trained on massive curated corpora. For crystalline stability, GNoME trains large graph models and active-learning pipelines to propose millions of candidate structures and flag hundreds of thousands as likely stable—establishing that data+scale can systematically widen the known inorganic universe [merchant2023gnome]. In catalysis, the Open Catalyst efforts formalized realistic workloads: OC20 introduced 1.28M DFT relaxations and 265M single-point evaluations for adsorbate–surface energetics and created standardized tasks (IS2RE/IS2RS/S2EF) with stringent generalization splits; OC22 extended to oxide electrocatalysts relevant to OER with more realistic catalysts and targets [chanussot2021oc20, tran2023oc22]. New foundation-style datasets push further: OMat24 aggregates >110M DFT entries and releases strong baselines (e.g., Equiformer-V2) that achieve near-chemical-accuracy on multiple targets [barrosoluque2024omat24]; OMol25 analogously scales molecular DFT data to >100M calculations spanning tens of millions of unique molecules, enabling broad pretraining for small-molecule physics [levine2025omol25]. Complementing datasets, foundation models like the universal model of atoms (UMA) and Orb explore single architectures that transfer across chemistry and tasks, aiming for cross-domain generalization with shared tokenization/featurization of atoms and local environments [wood2025uma, orbitalmaterials2025orb]. These surrogates excel at S1–S2 targets (bulk stability, adsorption energies, local structural relaxations) but are largely D1–D2 in operation: fixed-form predictors trained on equilibrium data, with limited capacity to reason about kinetics, synthesis windows, or device-level constraints that emerge at S3–S4. The net effect is that they remain superb "atoms-to-properties" engines, yet they do not autonomously help solve the long-horizon, multi-paper evidence assembly and process-aware planning needed, from atomic scale to device scale rationales [merchant2023gnome, chanussot2021oc20, tran2023oc22, barrosoluque2024omat24, levine2025omol25, wood2025uma].

Domain LLMs span three useful roles. (i) Materials-text models (MatSciBERT/MatBERT/MaterialBERT) are trained on materials corpora to power entity/relation extraction, document classification, and graph building; MatSciBERT outperforms SciBERT on named entity recognition (NER) and relation tasks across curated benchmarks, while MatBERT shows that domain-specific pretraining significantly lifts NER F1 and sample efficiency in materials texts; MaterialBERT introduces a domain tokenizer/vocabulary tuned to materials literature, while Intern-S1 scales domain-specific reasoning capabilities [gupta2022matscibert, trewartha2022quantifying, yoshitake2022materialbert, internlm2025interns1]. (ii) Chemical/polymer LLMs target sequence-level prediction/generation: ChemBERTa established transformer baselines and scaling trends for SMILES; ChemBERTa-2 pushed to 77M SMILES and showed consistent gains (and that multi-task regression pretraining can beat MLM (Masked Language Modeling) in transfer); ChemBERTa-3 contributes to open, end-to-end training infrastructure for chemical foundation models; MegaMolBART provides a large-scale generative sequence model optimized for molecular design, with MOL-Mamba introducing state-space models for efficient representation [chithrananda2020chemberta, ahmad2022chemberta2, singh2025chemberta3, nvidia2022megamolbart, hu2025molmamba]. ChemGPT demonstrates generative scaling to >1B parameters with clear neural-scaling laws for chemical LLMs, clarifying how model/data scale trade off in practice [frey2023neural]. In polymers, TransPolymer introduces a chemically-aware tokenizer and MLM pretraining that improves regression performances across ten benchmarks; polyBERT builds an end-to-end, ultrafast pipeline and screens 100M hypothetical polymers; PolyNC fuses natural-language and chemical-sequence inputs to improve unified polymer property prediction [xu2023transpolymer, kuenneth2023polybert, qiu2024polync]. (iii) Generative/design LLMs for materials include ChatMOF and the GPT-4 Reticular Chemist for MOF proposals [kang2024chatmof, zheng2023gpt4], CataLM for catalyst design [wang2024catalm]; Crystal-LLM (autoregressive) generates crystal structures from composition, and MatterGen scales inorganic structure generation with validated discoveries and robust property control [kang2024chatmof, antunes2024crystallm, zeni2025generative]. Collectively these models deliver flexible text/code/structure interfaces and strong S1–S2 performance—ideal for curation, candidate suggestion, or surrogate-assisted screening—but they are typically short-horizon (D1–D2): they answer prompts, not conduct hours-long, tool-grounded, hierarchical inquiry across conflicting literature [yoshitake2022materialbert, trewartha2022quantifying, gupta2022matscibert, qiu2024polync, kuenneth2023polybert, xu2023transpolymer, chithrananda2020chemberta, ahmad2022chemberta2, singh2025chemberta3, frey2023neural, nvidia2022megamolbart, kang2024chatmof, zeni2025generative, antunes2024crystallm].

children.heading: A.3 Agentic systems for scientific inquiry

content.text: Agent frameworks aim to orchestrate end-to-end inquiry: decompose goals, retrieve and reconcile evidence, use domain tools/simulators, and iteratively critique/plan. Early exemplars used rule/graph planning and Bayesian loops within constrained scopes—Chematica/SYNTHIA operationalized expert retrosynthesis rules and heuristic search; CAMD framed autonomous design/make/test/learn for materials screening [merck\_synthia\_website, montoya2020camd]. LLM-based agents extend this with language-native decomposition and tool-use: ChemCrow connects models to chemistry tools (e.g., RDKit, databases) to complete realistic tasks [bran2024chemcrow]; HoneyComb provides a flexible materials-agent stack with retrieval/tooling and HPC hooks [zhang2024honeycomb]; SciAgents formalizes multi-agent graph reasoning for scientific planning [ghafarollahi2025sciagents]. Recent hierarchical frameworks like El Agente introduce orchestration for complex quantum chemistry workflows [zou2025elagente], while systems such as CheMatAgent, ChemAgent, MatAgent, and ChemHAS further specialize in tool learning and human-in-the-loop coordination [wu2025chematagent, tang2025chemagent, bazgir2025matagent, li2025chemhas]. Finally, “AI co-scientist” frameworks couple planning with web/code tools and emphasize evaluation and provenance [gottweis2025towards]. Execution back-ends close the loop: A-Lab and RoboMapper demonstrate self-driving labs discovering and characterizing new materials [szymanski2023alab, wang2023sustainable]; IBM RXN/RoboRXN links digital retrosynthesis with automated synthesis [ibm2020roborxn]; and NVIDIA ALCHEMI targets scaled infrastructure (data, models, and accelerated simulation) for materials discovery [ong2025alchemi]. Despite progress, most agents today operate at D2–D3 depth and S1–S3 scope; they rarely sustain thousand-query retrieval runs, explicit topic-tree governance, or tight coupling to cross-domain process constraints that S3–S4 device problems demand. This is precisely the niche for deep-research agents: to deliver hierarchical planning, multi-stage local+web retrieval at scale, targeted tool/simulator calls, and systematic self-critique with dense provenance until a decision-ready synthesis emerges [merck\_synthia\_website, montoya2020camd, bran2024chemcrow, zhang2024honeycomb, ghafarollahi2025sciagents, gottweis2025towards, szymanski2023alab, ibm2020roborxn, ong2025alchemi].

children.heading: A.4 Gap to deep research at S3–S4/D4

content.text: Despite existing progress, the transition to S3–S4 nano-device complexity poses a fundamental barrier. The combinatorial explosion across materials, interfaces, processing parameters, and operational constraints creates hypothesis spaces where decisive insights lie at the intersections of disparate literature, conflicting reports, and cross-domain phenomena. Crucially, long-horizon, hierarchical evidence accumulation (D4) remains under-documented: many agents cap at D2–D3, with limited iterative loops, shallow coordination, and no explicit topic-tree control for breadth-then-depth synthesis. Commercial deep-research offerings introduced in 2025 enable multi-step inquiry but remain closed-source with limited controllability and local integration, reinforcing the need for open, on-prem frameworks tailored to proprietary materials workflows. DToR addresses this by treating each research node as an evidence-grounded state in a resource-bounded tree search, bridging the symbolic reasoning of ToT/GoT with the domain knowledge grounding required for scientific discovery. To our knowledge, DToR is the first open, on-prem framework that explicitly couples local domain RAG with gap-triggered web expansion within a resource-bounded tree to address S3–S4 materials discovery—a regime where neither pure surrogates nor closed commercial DR agents operate reliably.

children.heading: Appendix D Local DR Experimental Settings
D.1 Open-source LLMs and local RAG corpus

content.text: We implement the framework in LangGraph and deploy three low-deployment-cost, open-source LLMs—DeepSeek-R1-14B, DeepSeek-R1-70B, QwQ-32B, gpt-oss-20B, and gpt-oss-120B—served locally via Ollama. All agent prompts and tool I/O use a JSON/tool-calling discipline for determinism and easy parsing, and the same research node (RN) described in Algorithm 2 is the unit of work in the controller (Algorithm 3 DToR). To provision representative, application-driven knowledge for nanomaterials and devices, we build a standardized Chroma vector store spanning 1,136,297 full-text papers organized around four pillars: sensors, batteries, catalysis, and semiconductors. The corpus is queried first under a local-first RAG policy; complementary web retrieval is invoked only when Algorithm 2 (local evidence-first)’s reflection detects unresolved knowledge gaps. Consistent with our emphasis on report-level usefulness rather than information retrieval (IR) benchmarking, the local-first RAG layer is treated as a routine, swappable component; DToR only triggers complementary web evidence upon explicit knowledge gaps and resolves cross-source conflicts by evidence majority → recency → domain authority. To make domain coverage portable and auditable without exposing any local texts or indices, we release the exact domain-scoping query templates corresponding to these four pillars. In practice we provide templates for sensors, energy/environment (covering batteries), semiconductors, and catalysis so others can target the same scope with their own holdings while keeping the orchestration identical.

Raw full texts are normalized with a cleaning pipeline designed for scientific documents at scale. The cleaner (i) preserves section structure and headers, (ii) retains LaTeX/MathJax equations and common math environments via stable markers, (iii) standardizes tables into a compact textual schema, (iv) normalizes URLs/DOIs and citation markers instead of stripping them, and (v) removes XML/HTML artifacts and noisy back matter conservatively. For long inputs, we apply sliding-window tokenization (default window8192 tokens, stride 4096) or a section-aware variant that respects detected boundaries, yielding JSONL suitable for downstream training or indexing. As our focus is on the DToR orchestration, we adhere to widely used, off-the-shelf preparation and vector-indexing practices; the corpus layer functions as a routine, swappable component rather than a methodological contribution. To enable scope-equivalent replication across different holdings, we release the exact domain-scoping query templates for sensors, energy/environment (including batteries), semiconductors, and catalysis; users may instantiate a local store with their customary institutional pipelines and preferred indexers.

Cleaned texts are split with a recursive character splitter (default chunk size 2500, overlap 500) and embedded using BAAI/bge-m3. Each chunk carries rich metadata (paper id, DOI, chunk id/index, source path, shard id) to support provenance and de-duplication. Embeddings are persisted in Chroma, enabling fast k-NN retrieval and incremental persistence during large ingestions. For robustness across machines, the store is partitioned into 500 volumes (shards). This organization serves two purposes: (1) controllable breadth—DToR can expand to additional volumes when the analyst decides to broaden coverage—and (2) bounded depth/latency—branches can be pruned once depth or evidence sufficiency is reached, without touching unrelated volumes. To mitigate licensing and privacy risk, our local corpus is restricted to institutionally licensed or open sources, and we release only the domain-scoping query templates—not texts or indices—so others can replicate scope without redistributing copyrighted content or PII.

In each research node, local retrieval is attempted first; summaries are synthesized from local evidence. Only when reflection surfaces concrete gaps does the controller expand (selecting additional volumes and spawning new RNs) or prune (stopping further growth of a branch). This strategy couples breadth (multi-volume exploration across pillars) with depth (iterative drilling within a volume) while keeping costs predictable on commodity hardware and avoiding external dependencies during the main research loop.

By default, we run all agents in a local-first configuration with cost-aware web fallback. Concretely, both single-agent DR and DToR branches use a research depth of 3 iterations, each RN queries the local Chroma first with top-k = 5, and only then invokes web search—by default DuckDuckGo—to avoid API fees. In DToR mode, breadth–depth is bounded with max branches = 3, max branch depth = 3, nodes per branch = 100, and a global cap of 500 nodes per experiment, ensuring predictable latency and compute. Models are served locally via Ollama; RAG is enabled by default with BAAI/bge-m3 embeddings, and we preserve document fidelity via full-page fetch and safe output hygiene. All parameters remain user-tunable through the configuration/RunnableConfig to trade off coverage, latency, and cost—for example, increasing depth or top-k for harder queries, or switching web backends when budgets permit.

The templates below define the *domain coverage* used by our local-first pipeline (sensors, energy/environment, semiconductors, catalysis). They are released to enable others to target the same topic scope with their own collections and entitlements.

E.1 LLM-as-Judge Rubric Prompt (applied to DR Report)

content.text: Now please analyze and evaluate the Report above on five equally weighted dimensions:

1. 1. Relevance to the stated objective, 2. 2. Depth and rigor of validation and benchmarking protocols, 3. 3. Clarity and reproducibility of methodology, 4. 4. Practical applicability and implementation readiness, 5. 5. Novelty and breadth of candidate coverage.
Depth and rigor of validation and benchmarking protocols,
Novelty and breadth of candidate coverage.

For each dimension, assign a score from 0–10 and supply a one-sentence justification. This rubric places equal emphasis on procedural rigor and clear implementation steps alongside overall alignment, ensuring that reports with well-defined benchmarks and actionable guidance receive full credit. The five-dimensional rubric was specifically designed to reward not just information retrieval but true research utility—prioritizing actionable insights with clear provenance over mere comprehensiveness.

Inter-rater reliability. We compute Pearson and Spearman correlations across judges over repeated topic–report evaluations; these correlations quantify *consistency among judges* and are *not* used as evidence of factual correctness. While the rubric emphasizes objective dimensions like novelty and applicability, potential LLM judge biases—such as favoring outputs from similar architectures—were mitigated by averaging across diverse models.

children.heading: E.1.1 Definitions of the Five Dimensions (equal weights)

content.text: Relevance = Alignment to the stated objective and scope, including coverage of key subcomponents rather than topic keywords alone. Depth = Rigor of analysis and validation (e.g., explicit assumptions, benchmarking or ablations, uncertainty/limitations stated). Clarity = Structure and reproducibility of the methodology, with traceable provenance (citations, data/sources, steps) and unambiguous claims. Applicability = Actionability of the outputs (materials/candidates, parameters/protocols, resource requirements) enabling near-term implementation. Novelty = Non-trivial ideas or candidate combinations beyond canonical baselines, with rationale, plus *breadth* of candidate coverage across the design space.

children.heading: E.2.2 Selectivity Scoring for PFAS Sensor Performance

content.text: The practical deployment of PFAS sensors demands not only strong binding to target per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances but also selective discrimination against common environmental interferents. To quantitatively evaluate this selectivity, we developed a unified scoring framework applicable to both static DFT calculations and explicit-solvent AIMD simulations, enabling direct comparison between computational methodologies while maintaining thermodynamic rigor. Selectivity Metric Derivation: The fundamental selectivity metric Δ​Δ​E\Delta\Delta E quantifies the differential binding preference between PFAS compounds and interferent molecules:

where Δ​E¯PFAS\overline{\Delta E}\_{\text{PFAS}} represents the average binding energy across four representative PFAS compounds (PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, and PFHxS), and Δ​E¯Interf\overline{\Delta E}\_{\text{Interf}} denotes the average binding energy for interferent species (humic acid and SDS), as illustrated in Figure [S14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F14 "Figure S14 ‣ E.2.2 Selectivity Scoring for PFAS Sensor Performance ‣ E.2 A/B Dueling Prompt ( DR Report A vs. DR Report B ) ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"). A larger positive Δ​Δ​E\Delta\Delta E value indicates superior selectivity, signifying stronger preferential binding to PFAS over interferents. For static DFT calculations, Δ​E\Delta E values correspond to the conventional binding energies Δ​Ebind\Delta E\_{\text{bind}} computed under implicit solvent conditions (Figure [S15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F15 "Figure S15 ‣ E.2.2 Selectivity Scoring for PFAS Sensor Performance ‣ E.2 A/B Dueling Prompt ( DR Report A vs. DR Report B ) ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). In explicit-solvent AIMD simulations, these are replaced by the time-averaged end-state potential energy gaps Δ​EpotES\Delta E\_{\text{pot}}^{\text{ES}}, which capture solvent reorganization effects and hydrogen-bonding network rearrangements absent from static calculations (Figures [S16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F16 "Figure S16 ‣ E.2.2 Selectivity Scoring for PFAS Sensor Performance ‣ E.2 A/B Dueling Prompt ( DR Report A vs. DR Report B ) ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery") and [S17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F17 "Figure S17 ‣ E.2.2 Selectivity Scoring for PFAS Sensor Performance ‣ E.2 A/B Dueling Prompt ( DR Report A vs. DR Report B ) ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). Linear Selectivity Scoring Framework: To enable meaningful comparison across candidate systems and computational methods, we normalize the selectivity metrics to a common scoring scale:

where Δ​Δ​Eβ​-CD\Delta\Delta E\_{\beta\text{-CD}} represents the selectivity of β\beta-cyclodextrin, our domain benchmark reference with established PFAS binding capability [wang2024reversible]. The sensitivity parameter β=0.2\beta=0.2 was selected to provide appropriate score discrimination while maintaining numerical stability across both DFT and AIMD datasets. This linear transformation preserves the physical meaning of energy differences while establishing β\beta-CD as the baseline reference (Score = 100). Comparative Analysis of Selectivity Under Different Solvation Models: The application of this unified scoring framework reveals striking differences between implicit and explicit solvation treatments. In static DFT calculations with implicit solvent, system A1 achieves the highest selectivity score of 102.4, outstandingly exceeding the β\beta-CD baseline (Figure [S18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F18 "Figure S18 ‣ E.2.2 Selectivity Scoring for PFAS Sensor Performance ‣ E.2 A/B Dueling Prompt ( DR Report A vs. DR Report B ) ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). The B-series candidates also prove competitive as B2 and B3 also showed slightly passing 100 score.

However, the inclusion of explicit water molecules and dynamic sampling in AIMD simulations dramatically alters the selectivity landscape (Figure [S19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F19 "Figure S19 ‣ E.2.2 Selectivity Scoring for PFAS Sensor Performance ‣ E.2 A/B Dueling Prompt ( DR Report A vs. DR Report B ) ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). Most notably, the majority of the candidate systems’ scores are below the β\beta-CD baseline in explicit solvent, with only B1 achieving the highest relative performance at 102.0. This systematic reduction in scores reflects the critical role of solvent-mediated effects: competitive water adsorption at binding sites, strong hydration of anionic PFAS headgroups, and the entropic penalties associated with constraining flexible molecules in adsorbed configurations. The reversal of relative rankings between static DFT and AIMD calculations—particularly the superior performance of B-series candidates under explicit solvation—underscores the importance of including solvent dynamics in sensor design evaluation. While static calculations provide valuable initial screening, the explicit-solvent AIMD results more accurately capture the complex interplay between adsorbate–surface interactions and solvent reorganization that governs selectivity under realistic aqueous conditions. Implications for Sensor Design: The divergence between implicit and explicit solvent results carries significant implications for PFAS sensor development. Systems optimized solely based on static DFT calculations may exhibit diminished selectivity in aqueous environments due to unforeseen solvent competition effects. Conversely, candidates that appear suboptimal in vacuum or implicit solvent calculations may benefit from favorable solvent-mediated interactions that enhance their practical selectivity. This highlights the necessity of multi-scale computational approaches that progress from efficient static screening to rigorous explicit-solvent validation for promising candidates.

The linear selectivity scoring framework presented here provides a quantitative, thermodynamically grounded metric for evaluating sensor performance across computational methodologies. By maintaining consistent notation and normalization across static and dynamic simulations, this approach enables systematic comparison of candidate materials while preserving the physical interpretability of the underlying energy differences.

children.heading: E.3.2 Multi-Metric Evaluation of PFAS Degradation Catalysts

content.text: Effective catalytic degradation of PFAS compounds requires both strong surface adsorption to concentrate the pollutants and sufficient activation of the exceptionally stable C–F bonds. To comprehensively evaluate candidate catalysts for PFAS degradation, we employed a three-pronged computational assessment framework encompassing static binding energies, explicit-solvent dynamics, and C–F bond dissociation energetics, with Ti4O7 serving as the domain benchmark reference [lin2018ti4o7].

The degradation performance evaluation integrates three complementary metrics that capture distinct aspects of the catalytic process. First, the binding energy Δ​Ebind\Delta E\_{\text{bind}} from static DFT calculations quantifies the thermodynamic driving force for PFAS adsorption onto catalyst surfaces (Figure [S22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F22 "Figure S22 ‣ E.3.2 Multi-Metric Evaluation of PFAS Degradation Catalysts ‣ E.3 PFAS Degradation ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). Strong binding ensures sufficient surface coverage and residence time for subsequent degradation reactions. Second, the explicit-solvent potential energy gap Δ​EpotES\Delta E\_{\text{pot}}^{\text{ES}} from AIMD simulations reveals how aqueous solvation affects the adsorption thermodynamics (Figures [S26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F26 "Figure S26 ‣ E.3.2 Multi-Metric Evaluation of PFAS Degradation Catalysts ‣ E.3 PFAS Degradation ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery") and [S27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F27 "Figure S27 ‣ E.3.2 Multi-Metric Evaluation of PFAS Degradation Catalysts ‣ E.3 PFAS Degradation ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")), accounting for competitive water adsorption and hydrogen-bonding network reorganization that static calculations cannot capture. Third, the C–F bond dissociation energy quantifies the activation barrier for the rate-limiting defluorination step, computed by displacing fluorine atoms from adsorbed PFAS configurations to isolated positions within the supercell (Figure [S23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F23 "Figure S23 ‣ E.3.2 Multi-Metric Evaluation of PFAS Degradation Catalysts ‣ E.3 PFAS Degradation ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). Scoring Framework for Degradation Performance
To enable quantitative comparison across these diverse metrics, we applied a unified linear scoring framework:

where Δmetric\Delta\_{\text{metric}} represents the performance differential relative to the Ti4O7 baseline, defined as Δ​E¯−Δ​E¯Ti4​O7\Delta\bar{E}-\Delta\bar{E}\_{\text{Ti}\_{4}\text{O}\_{7}} for binding metrics and Δ​E¯Ti4​O7−Δ​E¯\Delta\bar{E}\_{\text{Ti}\_{4}\text{O}\_{7}}-\Delta\bar{E} for C–F dissociation. Here Δ​E¯\Delta\bar{E} is the mean energy value averaged over four representative PFAS compounds (PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, PFHxS), and β=0.2\beta=0.2 serves as the sensitivity parameter. For binding metrics (both static DFT and AIMD), stronger adsorption (corresponding to larger magnitude binding energies) yields higher scores. For C–F dissociation, lower energy barriers yield higher scores, reflecting more facile bond activation. The distribution of C–F dissociation energies across different PFAS compounds and candidate surfaces exhibits substantial variability (Figure [S24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F24 "Figure S24 ‣ E.3.2 Multi-Metric Evaluation of PFAS Degradation Catalysts ‣ E.3 PFAS Degradation ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")), with mean values ranging from approximately 2 to 6 eV (Figure [S25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F25 "Figure S25 ‣ E.3.2 Multi-Metric Evaluation of PFAS Degradation Catalysts ‣ E.3 PFAS Degradation ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). This variation underscores the importance of averaging over multiple PFAS species to obtain representative performance metrics, as individual compounds may exhibit preferential interactions with specific surface sites or crystallographic facets. Performance Analysis Across Computational Methods

Application of this scoring framework reveals distinct performance patterns across the three evaluation metrics. In static DFT calculations, several candidates demonstrate superior PFAS binding relative to the Ti4O7 benchmark (Figure [S28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F28 "Figure S28 ‣ E.3.2 Multi-Metric Evaluation of PFAS Degradation Catalysts ‣ E.3 PFAS Degradation ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")), with C-series materials generally exhibiting stronger adsorption energies. However, the inclusion of explicit solvent effects in AIMD simulations significantly alters these rankings (Figure [S30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F30 "Figure S30 ‣ E.3.2 Multi-Metric Evaluation of PFAS Degradation Catalysts ‣ E.3 PFAS Degradation ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")), with most candidates showing reduced binding scores due to solvent-mediated destabilization effects. This divergence highlights the critical importance of accounting for aqueous solvation in evaluating catalyst performance under realistic conditions. The C–F bond activation scores (Figure [S29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F29 "Figure S29 ‣ E.3.2 Multi-Metric Evaluation of PFAS Degradation Catalysts ‣ E.3 PFAS Degradation ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")) provide complementary insights into degradation potential. Notably, candidates that excel in binding may not necessarily facilitate efficient C–F bond cleavage, as these properties depend on distinct electronic and geometric factors. However, C-series materials were proven in average level better with lower F dissociation energy barriers. Nonetheless, the ideal degradation catalyst must balance strong PFAS adsorption with effective bond activation—a trade-off that our multi-metric scoring framework quantitatively captures. Implications for Catalyst Design

The comprehensive evaluation framework presented here reveals that no single candidate uniformly excels across all performance metrics. Strong surface binding, while essential for PFAS capture, does not guarantee facile C–F bond activation. Similarly, materials optimized for bond dissociation may suffer from weak adsorption, particularly under aqueous conditions where solvent competition is significant. This multi-dimensional performance landscape emphasizes the need for balanced catalyst design that considers both thermodynamic (binding) and kinetic (bond activation) factors, evaluated under both implicit and explicit solvation conditions to ensure robust performance predictions for practical applications. As indicated in this dry lab study, A3, B2, C3, and C4 could be promising candidates for further investigation in wet lab.

The performance scoring normalized to the PVDF baseline (Figures [S35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F35 "Figure S35 ‣ E.4.2 Battery Binder Adhesion Performance ‣ E.4 Battery Binder ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery") and [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#footnote6 "footnote 6 ‣ Figure S36 ‣ E.4.2 Battery Binder Adhesion Performance ‣ E.4 Battery Binder ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")) quantifies this wet-interface reordering: candidates optimized for dry adhesion may underperform under operating electrolyte conditions, whereas others show unexpected compatibility. These results underscore the need for explicit-solvent, potential-controlled calculations in binder screening, since interfacial energetics in liquid electrolytes are governed by solvent layering, ion crowding, and potential-dependent desolvation that vacuum or implicit-solvent models cannot capture.

Abstract
chunks.text:
###### Abstract

We present a long-horizon, hierarchical deep research (DR) agent designed for complex materials and device discovery problems that exceed the scope of existing Machine Learning (ML) surrogates and closed-source commercial agents. Our framework instantiates a locally deployable DR instance that integrates local retrieval-augmented generation with large language model reasoners, enhanced by a Deep Tree of Research (DToR) mechanism that adaptively expands and prunes research branches to maximize coverage, depth, and coherence. We systematically evaluate across 27 nanomaterials/device topics using a large language model (LLM)-as-judge rubric with five web-enabled state-of-the-art models as jurors. In addition, we conduct dry-lab validations on five representative tasks, where human experts use domain simulations (e.g., density functional theory, DFT) to verify whether DR-agent proposals are actionable. Results show that our DR agent produces reports with quality comparable to— and often exceeding— those of commercial systems (ChatGPT-5-thinking/o3/o4-mini-high Deep Research) at a substantially lower cost, while enabling on-prem integration with local data and tools.

Keywords: deep research, hierarchical reasoning, materials discovery, retrieval-augmented generation, large language models, computational materials science, autonomous agents

## 1 Introduction

Machine learning (ML) for nanomaterials and device discovery has advanced from tractable single-entity predictions to increasingly complex, system-level challenges. At the molecular or crystal level (S1), modern surrogates routinely predict intrinsic properties [xie2018cgcnn]. Small assemblies (S2)—interfaces, heterostructures, or simple 2–3-component devices—introduce coupling effects yet remain manageable. Real-world nano-devices, however, operate at system scope (S3): multi-layer perovskite stacks with interdependent layers, core–shell–doped catalysts with engineered interfaces, or nano-architected battery electrodes where transport across length scales governs performance [severson2019cyclelife]. The ultimate challenge lies in cross-domain integration (S4): platforms that span material families, recognition chemistries, and transduction modalities—for example, engineering 2D-material field-effect transistor (FET) sensors with aptamer functionalization for environmental detection [szymanski2023alab, wang2022aptamer\_gfet].

Meeting this escalation in scope requires a matching escalation in depth. We frame depth from single-pass prediction/forward screening (D1), to multi-stage pipelines with structured outputs (D2), to long-horizon synthesis with iterative planning (D3), and ultimately hierarchical, breadth–depth exploration (D4). While recent agentic frameworks have successfully demonstrated hierarchical orchestration for complex scientific workflows [gottweis2025towards, ghafarollahi2025sciagents, zou2025elagente], ensuring robust execution and simulation management, device/system-level optimization and design (S3–S4) presents a distinct challenge. The governing laws for device integration are not fully encoded in standard simulation packages, requiring long-horizon hierarchical autonomous discovery (D3–D4) with potential to navigate the combinatorial explosion of processing parameters sparsely distributed across heterogeneous knowledge sources. Existing approaches typically face limitations in this unstructured knowledge regime [montoya2020camd, merchant2023gnome, chanussot2021oc20, levine2025omol25] (Detailed in Appendix [A](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A1 "Appendix A Related Work in Physics ML Surrogates, Domain LLMs, and Agentic Systems ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")).

To address this gap, we introduce a hierarchical deep-research (DR) agent111We use *Deep Research (DR)* to denote a single-threaded, iterative retrieval–reasoning–writing loop run by one agent. *Deep Tree of Research (DToR)* denotes a tree-structured orchestration that spawns and selects among multiple DR branches with hierarchical planning and merge. Throughout, ”hierarchical deep research” is synonymous with DToR; we henceforth use only DR and DToR for clarity. purpose-built for long-horizon scientific inquiry. Given a natural-language inquiry, the system instantiates a locally deployable DR instance that iterates between local and web retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and large language model (LLM) reasoners (summarizers, reflectors). We further expand the DR instance into a Deep Tree of Research (DToR) where each instance is treated as a node in a tree-structured workflow. DToR adaptively expands/prunes branches to improve coverage, depth, and coherence. The agent is self-directed/navigated (plans its own research path), runs locally for controllability and privacy, and targets S3–S4 hypotheses. At a glance, our goal is to measure synthesis quality by a programmatic evaluation harness (anchored rubric, A/B preferences) plus dry-lab checks. We then show that orchestration via DToR consistently improves synthesis quality over single-instance DR across model backbones and local-corpus budgets at comparable compute.

Contributions. (1) A democratized, locally deployable framework for scientific deep research, enabling materials researchers to exercise fine-grained control over cost and preferences using open-source LLMs while achieving performance that surpasses commercial state-of-the-art solutions in most cases (§[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S3 "3 Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). (2) A hierarchical orchestration (DToR) that yields robust gains over single-instance DR across LLM backbones and local data budgets, supported by comprehensive factorial and targeted component ablations. (3) An evaluation program combining anchored rubric scores, repeated A/B duels, and dry-lab validation to assess synthesis quality.

### 1.1 Related work

Recent work on structured reasoning for LLMs has moved beyond linear prompting toward explicit search structures. Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) frames inference as a branching search over intermediate ‘thoughts’, while Graph-of-Thoughts (GoT) generalizes this to arbitrary graphs to model non-linear dependencies and subproblem coordination [yao2023tree, besta2024graph, yao2024effectivegot]. In parallel, reason–act and self-improvement paradigms—ReAct, Reflexion, and Self-Refine—provide strong baselines for multi-step decision-making and revision ([yao2022react, shinn2023reflexion, madaan2023selfrefine]). Foundational web-agent environments/benchmarks—BrowseComp, WebLINX, WebArena, and BrowserGym—formalize browsing/navigation competencies and support reproducible evaluation [wei2025browsecomp, pan2024weblinx, zhou2023webarena, lesellier2024browsergym]. Work on retrieval is also moving toward more adaptive strategies: Self-RAG [asai2024selfrag] learns when to retrieve and critique outputs, CRAG [yan2024crag] evaluates retrieval quality and escalates to web search when evidence is weak, and GraphRAG [peng2024graphragsurvey] uses graph-structured knowledge for non-flat retrieval. Despite this progress, there is no framework that unifies structured branching and adaptive retrieval in a way that scales under practical compute and data limits for domain-specific research settings.

## 2 Method

D4 requires structured and budget-aware planning beyond short-term queries. We introduce DToR, a breadth-then-depth controller for DR that starts from multiple parallel perspectives, selectively expands or prunes based on explicit gap checks, runs evidence-first research steps (local RAG with adapted web search), and produces source-grounded reports.

### 2.1 Single DR Instance

As shown in Fig. [S1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F1 "Figure S1 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")222Supporting figures (S1–S13) illustrating detailed experimental results and supplementary analyses are presented in Appendix [B](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2 "Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"). (with comparison against common standard DR agent [langchain2025localdeepresearcher]), each DR instance is an evidence-first loop that (1) generates a search query; (2) performs local RAG; (3) summarizes local evidence; (4) generates a complementary query to induce topical diversity; (5) conducts web research for both queries; (6) integrates/updates previous retrieved segments in a running summary; (7) reflects to propose follow-up query. The process would loop until a set maximum round before (8) finalizing. Three design choices distinguish this instance from common local DR agents[langchain2025localdeepresearcher] which only conduct (1)-(5)-(6)-(7): local-first retrieval (before web) to reduce drift, hallucination, and surface domain priors; diversity-aware query generation (local summary derived complementary query) to guarantee comprehensiveness; and robust I/O discipline to prevent controller stalls on local-hosted LLMs. Compared with classic ReAct/Reflexion-style linear loops, this instance adds an explicit breadth mechanism and escalation policy akin to adaptive/corrective-RAG, while remaining compatible with the drop-in alternative RAG methods.

2.2 DToR: from perspectives to gap-driven expansion
chunks.text:
### 2.2 DToR: from perspectives to gap-driven expansion

Based on the single DR instance, we treat each DR instance as a Research Node (RN) inside a branch-and-bound controller (Fig. [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Method ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). Starting from a user query, a diversifier proposes several orthogonal Perspectives (P1, P2…)—each seeds one branch with a budget: maximum depth, nodes per branch, and total branches. For the active branch, the router (i) runs the next pending RN (the single DR instance), producing a RN summary; (ii) invokes analyst based on remaining depth/budget/current RN report quality to give a decision EXPAND, PRUNE; and, if EXPAND with budget remaining, (iii) invokes knowledge gap explorer to materializes new RNs from this RN targeted to those gaps (depth+1) and updates remaining budget. Branches that stagnate are pruned; (iv) branches that reach depth or converge are synthesized into a perspective report. When all branches reach synthesis, a final synthesizer reconciles cross-branch evidence, resolves conflicts, and outputs a provenance-rich, consolidated report. Conceptually, this is a tree-of-search over (query, evidence, summary) states rather than over purely symbolic "thoughts," inheriting the benefits of structured exploration/backtracking from tree/graph-based reasoning while remaining tailored to information-seeking and citation fidelity under explicit resource budgets.
