### 3.1 Experimental setup

We evaluate across 27 expert-crafted topics spanning materials and devices (e.g., per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) FET probes, CO2 sensing in 2D materials, Li/Na-selective membranes, CO2-reduction catalysts); full topic prompts are provided in Appendix [C](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A3 "Appendix C Nanomaterials and Device Topics ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"). For each topic, we consider 41 agents—11 commercial and 30 local (split evenly between single DR-instance and DToR-mode)—on consumer-level hardware. We evaluate local agents across LLM backbones (gpt-oss120B, gpt-oss20B, QwQ32B) and local RAG budgets (local0/local100/local500), holding orchestration fixed and varying only backbone and corpus size; full agent configurations in Appendix [D](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A4 "Appendix D Local DR Experimental Settings ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"). Using an LLM-as-judge protocol (Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5 "Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")), we generate 41 distinct report variants per topic and have five web-enabled SOTA judges—Claude 4 Opus (thinking), Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok-3 (thinking), ChatGPT-o3, and ChatGPT-o4-mini-high—score each report under a fixed, double-blind rubric (judges are blinded to agent identities) with five equally weighted dimensions—(1) relevance, (2) depth, (3) clarity, (4) applicability, and (5) novelty—whose concise definitions are provided in Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5 "Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery").

Judge view and anonymization: LLM judges see only the final report text—no agent/model identifiers, tool logs, or token/count metadata—and assign numeric scores on five anchored dimensions (relevance, depth/rigor, clarity/reproducibility, applicability, novelty) under a fixed instruction to “act as an experienced materials scientist” (Appendix [E](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5 "Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). The rubric provides positive/negative exemplars per dimension; unresolved contradictions or failure to reconcile conflicts between local and web evidence are penalized under Depth/Rigor and Clarity/Reproducibility, while reports that explicitly compare sources and justify a resolution are rewarded. Access to local vs. web contexts is controlled at generation time (agents run in local-only or web-enabled modes), whereas judges never see those contexts—only the synthesized report—so the evaluation targets synthesis/reasoning quality rather than retrieval exposure. Judges assign 0–10 per dimension with one-sentence justifications; numeric ratings are extracted by a deterministic parser. We repeat the evaluation three times per topic–report–judge combination, yielding 27×41×5×3=16,60527\times 41\times 5\times 3=16,605 rubric-based judgments. Inter-judge agreement (Pearson correlation on scores and Spearman rank correlation) remains high across all dimensions.

Within each pool we rank reports by rubric average and select the top-3; the resulting 9 reports then enter all pairwise duels ((92)=36\binom{9}{2}=36 pairs per topic). Duels are double-blind and order-randomized, guided by a concise “experienced materials scientist” prompt emphasizing clarity, gap prioritization, and actionable next steps. While dry-lab simulations provide an initial filter, looking more closely at the candidates proposed by the DR agents reveals a feasibility gap in current LLM–RAG orchestration(Fig. [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.2 Experimental results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). In PFAS sensing, the agents successfully identified rational designs like B1 and A1, yet DToR agent also produced “kitchen-sink” failures like C3, which stacks four mutually incompatible phases (hydrophobic fluorosilane, hydrophilic MXene, Ag nanoparticles, acidic PEDOT:PSS). In practice, synthesis of such a complex system would be infeasible, because the agents ignored likely colloidal incompatibilities (e.g., phase separation and acid-induced etching) that would render the device chemically unstable[cameron2020pedotpss, kumar2023mxenestability]. Similarly, for PFAS degradation, cost-effective and chemically robust candidates like C4 and A3 stand in contrast to C5, a triple heterostructure (MXene/g-C3N4/Al2O3) that neglects potential challenges in interfacial charge-transfer resistance and fabrication complexity[mandari2025gcn\_mxene\_review, bagnall2025al2o3\_stability]. These over-engineered failures stem from a fundamental limitation in current agent architectures: without intrinsic wet-lab feasibility priors, cost models, or external physics validators, LLMs are prone to “inverse-design hallucinations” [miret2025llms\_materials\_discovery, kalai2025hallucinate] that assume functional additivity where physical incompatibility exists. This underscores that future AI4Science frameworks must integrate dedicated domain-validator modules (e.g., synthesis-aware ReAct loops) to ground theoretical generation in experimental reality333Extended discussion with further citations is available in Appendix LABEL:candidate\_feasibility\_discussions..

All timings reflect a single-machine setup with serialized agent scheduling (energy estimation methodology in Appendix LABEL:app:power\_estimation); under this controlled setting, DToR with gpt-oss120B averages 19.6 h (Fig. [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 3.2 Experimental results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"), Fig. [S11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A2.F11 "Figure S11 ‣ Appendix B Supplementary Figures ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). Overall, our gains arise from orchestration and information coverage rather than “model pile-up”: users can explicitly tune for quality (DToR + corpus) or for cost/latency (DR/no-RAG) depending on resources. chunks.text:
## 4 Conclusion

We introduced DToR, a locally deployable DR agent with a resource-bounded tree controller that unifies local-first RAG, diversity-aware query generation, and gap-driven branching into provenance-rich, long-horizon information seeking. Across 27 topics and 41 agents, under 16,605 rubric judgments from 5 web-enabled judges, our best local model (DToR\_gpt-oss120B\_local500) ranked 1st (8.57/10) with a 79% mean duel win rate (14,580 dueling judgement) while using only 4.37 kWh/report on consumer devices. In dry-lab validation across five applications, its candidates matched or surpassed the best commercial solutions. This work highlights a practical path toward open, secure, and scalable on-prem DR agents for automated, accelerated scientific discovery at the S3–S4 level.

A.1 Physics-aligned surrogates and classical ML
chunks.text:
### A.1 Physics-aligned surrogates and classical ML

Physics-guided predictive surrogates now operate at web-scale, with graph networks and equivariant models trained on massive curated corpora. For crystalline stability, GNoME trains large graph models and active-learning pipelines to propose millions of candidate structures and flag hundreds of thousands as likely stable—establishing that data+scale can systematically widen the known inorganic universe [merchant2023gnome]. In catalysis, the Open Catalyst efforts formalized realistic workloads: OC20 introduced 1.28M DFT relaxations and 265M single-point evaluations for adsorbate–surface energetics and created standardized tasks (IS2RE/IS2RS/S2EF) with stringent generalization splits; OC22 extended to oxide electrocatalysts relevant to OER with more realistic catalysts and targets [chanussot2021oc20, tran2023oc22]. New foundation-style datasets push further: OMat24 aggregates >110M DFT entries and releases strong baselines (e.g., Equiformer-V2) that achieve near-chemical-accuracy on multiple targets [barrosoluque2024omat24]; OMol25 analogously scales molecular DFT data to >100M calculations spanning tens of millions of unique molecules, enabling broad pretraining for small-molecule physics [levine2025omol25]. Complementing datasets, foundation models like the universal model of atoms (UMA) and Orb explore single architectures that transfer across chemistry and tasks, aiming for cross-domain generalization with shared tokenization/featurization of atoms and local environments [wood2025uma, orbitalmaterials2025orb]. These surrogates excel at S1–S2 targets (bulk stability, adsorption energies, local structural relaxations) but are largely D1–D2 in operation: fixed-form predictors trained on equilibrium data, with limited capacity to reason about kinetics, synthesis windows, or device-level constraints that emerge at S3–S4. The net effect is that they remain superb "atoms-to-properties" engines, yet they do not autonomously help solve the long-horizon, multi-paper evidence assembly and process-aware planning needed, from atomic scale to device scale rationales [merchant2023gnome, chanussot2021oc20, tran2023oc22, barrosoluque2024omat24, levine2025omol25, wood2025uma].

A.2 Domain LLMs (non-agent)
chunks.text:
### A.2 Domain LLMs (non-agent)

Domain LLMs span three useful roles. (i) Materials-text models (MatSciBERT/MatBERT/MaterialBERT) are trained on materials corpora to power entity/relation extraction, document classification, and graph building; MatSciBERT outperforms SciBERT on named entity recognition (NER) and relation tasks across curated benchmarks, while MatBERT shows that domain-specific pretraining significantly lifts NER F1 and sample efficiency in materials texts; MaterialBERT introduces a domain tokenizer/vocabulary tuned to materials literature, while Intern-S1 scales domain-specific reasoning capabilities [gupta2022matscibert, trewartha2022quantifying, yoshitake2022materialbert, internlm2025interns1]. (ii) Chemical/polymer LLMs target sequence-level prediction/generation: ChemBERTa established transformer baselines and scaling trends for SMILES; ChemBERTa-2 pushed to 77M SMILES and showed consistent gains (and that multi-task regression pretraining can beat MLM (Masked Language Modeling) in transfer); ChemBERTa-3 contributes to open, end-to-end training infrastructure for chemical foundation models; MegaMolBART provides a large-scale generative sequence model optimized for molecular design, with MOL-Mamba introducing state-space models for efficient representation [chithrananda2020chemberta, ahmad2022chemberta2, singh2025chemberta3, nvidia2022megamolbart, hu2025molmamba]. ChemGPT demonstrates generative scaling to >1B parameters with clear neural-scaling laws for chemical LLMs, clarifying how model/data scale trade off in practice [frey2023neural]. In polymers, TransPolymer introduces a chemically-aware tokenizer and MLM pretraining that improves regression performances across ten benchmarks; polyBERT builds an end-to-end, ultrafast pipeline and screens 100M hypothetical polymers; PolyNC fuses natural-language and chemical-sequence inputs to improve unified polymer property prediction [xu2023transpolymer, kuenneth2023polybert, qiu2024polync]. (iii) Generative/design LLMs for materials include ChatMOF and the GPT-4 Reticular Chemist for MOF proposals [kang2024chatmof, zheng2023gpt4], CataLM for catalyst design [wang2024catalm]; Crystal-LLM (autoregressive) generates crystal structures from composition, and MatterGen scales inorganic structure generation with validated discoveries and robust property control [kang2024chatmof, antunes2024crystallm, zeni2025generative]. Collectively these models deliver flexible text/code/structure interfaces and strong S1–S2 performance—ideal for curation, candidate suggestion, or surrogate-assisted screening—but they are typically short-horizon (D1–D2): they answer prompts, not conduct hours-long, tool-grounded, hierarchical inquiry across conflicting literature [yoshitake2022materialbert, trewartha2022quantifying, gupta2022matscibert, qiu2024polync, kuenneth2023polybert, xu2023transpolymer, chithrananda2020chemberta, ahmad2022chemberta2, singh2025chemberta3, frey2023neural, nvidia2022megamolbart, kang2024chatmof, zeni2025generative, antunes2024crystallm].

A.3 Agentic systems for scientific inquiry
chunks.text:
### A.3 Agentic systems for scientific inquiry

Agent frameworks aim to orchestrate end-to-end inquiry: decompose goals, retrieve and reconcile evidence, use domain tools/simulators, and iteratively critique/plan. Early exemplars used rule/graph planning and Bayesian loops within constrained scopes—Chematica/SYNTHIA operationalized expert retrosynthesis rules and heuristic search; CAMD framed autonomous design/make/test/learn for materials screening [merck\_synthia\_website, montoya2020camd]. LLM-based agents extend this with language-native decomposition and tool-use: ChemCrow connects models to chemistry tools (e.g., RDKit, databases) to complete realistic tasks [bran2024chemcrow]; HoneyComb provides a flexible materials-agent stack with retrieval/tooling and HPC hooks [zhang2024honeycomb]; SciAgents formalizes multi-agent graph reasoning for scientific planning [ghafarollahi2025sciagents]. Recent hierarchical frameworks like El Agente introduce orchestration for complex quantum chemistry workflows [zou2025elagente], while systems such as CheMatAgent, ChemAgent, MatAgent, and ChemHAS further specialize in tool learning and human-in-the-loop coordination [wu2025chematagent, tang2025chemagent, bazgir2025matagent, li2025chemhas]. Finally, “AI co-scientist” frameworks couple planning with web/code tools and emphasize evaluation and provenance [gottweis2025towards]. Execution back-ends close the loop: A-Lab and RoboMapper demonstrate self-driving labs discovering and characterizing new materials [szymanski2023alab, wang2023sustainable]; IBM RXN/RoboRXN links digital retrosynthesis with automated synthesis [ibm2020roborxn]; and NVIDIA ALCHEMI targets scaled infrastructure (data, models, and accelerated simulation) for materials discovery [ong2025alchemi]. Despite progress, most agents today operate at D2–D3 depth and S1–S3 scope; they rarely sustain thousand-query retrieval runs, explicit topic-tree governance, or tight coupling to cross-domain process constraints that S3–S4 device problems demand. This is precisely the niche for deep-research agents: to deliver hierarchical planning, multi-stage local+web retrieval at scale, targeted tool/simulator calls, and systematic self-critique with dense provenance until a decision-ready synthesis emerges [merck\_synthia\_website, montoya2020camd, bran2024chemcrow, zhang2024honeycomb, ghafarollahi2025sciagents, gottweis2025towards, szymanski2023alab, ibm2020roborxn, ong2025alchemi].

### A.4 Gap to deep research at S3–S4/D4

Despite existing progress, the transition to S3–S4 nano-device complexity poses a fundamental barrier. The combinatorial explosion across materials, interfaces, processing parameters, and operational constraints creates hypothesis spaces where decisive insights lie at the intersections of disparate literature, conflicting reports, and cross-domain phenomena. Crucially, long-horizon, hierarchical evidence accumulation (D4) remains under-documented: many agents cap at D2–D3, with limited iterative loops, shallow coordination, and no explicit topic-tree control for breadth-then-depth synthesis. Commercial deep-research offerings introduced in 2025 enable multi-step inquiry but remain closed-source with limited controllability and local integration, reinforcing the need for open, on-prem frameworks tailored to proprietary materials workflows. DToR addresses this by treating each research node as an evidence-grounded state in a resource-bounded tree search, bridging the symbolic reasoning of ToT/GoT with the domain knowledge grounding required for scientific discovery. To our knowledge, DToR is the first open, on-prem framework that explicitly couples local domain RAG with gap-triggered web expansion within a resource-bounded tree to address S3–S4 materials discovery—a regime where neither pure surrogates nor closed commercial DR agents operate reliably.

### D.1 Open-source LLMs and local RAG corpus

We implement the framework in LangGraph and deploy three low-deployment-cost, open-source LLMs—DeepSeek-R1-14B, DeepSeek-R1-70B, QwQ-32B, gpt-oss-20B, and gpt-oss-120B—served locally via Ollama. All agent prompts and tool I/O use a JSON/tool-calling discipline for determinism and easy parsing, and the same research node (RN) described in Algorithm 2 is the unit of work in the controller (Algorithm 3 DToR). To provision representative, application-driven knowledge for nanomaterials and devices, we build a standardized Chroma vector store spanning 1,136,297 full-text papers organized around four pillars: sensors, batteries, catalysis, and semiconductors. The corpus is queried first under a local-first RAG policy; complementary web retrieval is invoked only when Algorithm 2 (local evidence-first)’s reflection detects unresolved knowledge gaps. Consistent with our emphasis on report-level usefulness rather than information retrieval (IR) benchmarking, the local-first RAG layer is treated as a routine, swappable component; DToR only triggers complementary web evidence upon explicit knowledge gaps and resolves cross-source conflicts by evidence majority → recency → domain authority. To make domain coverage portable and auditable without exposing any local texts or indices, we release the exact domain-scoping query templates corresponding to these four pillars. In practice we provide templates for sensors, energy/environment (covering batteries), semiconductors, and catalysis so others can target the same scope with their own holdings while keeping the orchestration identical.

D.1.1 Corpus construction

#### D.1.1 Corpus construction

Raw full texts are normalized with a cleaning pipeline designed for scientific documents at scale. The cleaner (i) preserves section structure and headers, (ii) retains LaTeX/MathJax equations and common math environments via stable markers, (iii) standardizes tables into a compact textual schema, (iv) normalizes URLs/DOIs and citation markers instead of stripping them, and (v) removes XML/HTML artifacts and noisy back matter conservatively. For long inputs, we apply sliding-window tokenization (default window8192 tokens, stride 4096) or a section-aware variant that respects detected boundaries, yielding JSONL suitable for downstream training or indexing. As our focus is on the DToR orchestration, we adhere to widely used, off-the-shelf preparation and vector-indexing practices; the corpus layer functions as a routine, swappable component rather than a methodological contribution. To enable scope-equivalent replication across different holdings, we release the exact domain-scoping query templates for sensors, energy/environment (including batteries), semiconductors, and catalysis; users may instantiate a local store with their customary institutional pipelines and preferred indexers.

Indexing and retrieval
chunks.text:
##### Indexing and retrieval

Cleaned texts are split with a recursive character splitter (default chunk size 2500, overlap 500) and embedded using BAAI/bge-m3. Each chunk carries rich metadata (paper id, DOI, chunk id/index, source path, shard id) to support provenance and de-duplication. Embeddings are persisted in Chroma, enabling fast k-NN retrieval and incremental persistence during large ingestions. For robustness across machines, the store is partitioned into 500 volumes (shards). This organization serves two purposes: (1) controllable breadth—DToR can expand to additional volumes when the analyst decides to broaden coverage—and (2) bounded depth/latency—branches can be pruned once depth or evidence sufficiency is reached, without touching unrelated volumes. ##### Agent Configuration

By default, we run all agents in a local-first configuration with cost-aware web fallback. Concretely, both single-agent DR and DToR branches use a research depth of 3 iterations, each RN queries the local Chroma first with top-k = 5, and only then invokes web search—by default DuckDuckGo—to avoid API fees. #### E.2.2 Selectivity Scoring for PFAS Sensor Performance

The practical deployment of PFAS sensors demands not only strong binding to target per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances but also selective discrimination against common environmental interferents. To quantitatively evaluate this selectivity, we developed a unified scoring framework applicable to both static DFT calculations and explicit-solvent AIMD simulations, enabling direct comparison between computational methodologies while maintaining thermodynamic rigor. Selectivity Metric Derivation: The fundamental selectivity metric Δ​Δ​E\Delta\Delta E quantifies the differential binding preference between PFAS compounds and interferent molecules:

Δ​Δ​E\Delta\Delta E

| | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | Δ​Δ​E=Δ​E¯PFAS−Δ​E¯Interf\Delta\Delta E=\overline{\Delta E}\_{\text{PFAS}}-\overline{\Delta E}\_{\text{Interf}} | | (1) |

Δ​Δ​E=Δ​E¯PFAS−Δ​E¯Interf\Delta\Delta E=\overline{\Delta E}_{\text{PFAS}}-\overline{\Delta E}_{\text{Interf}}

where Δ​E¯PFAS\overline{\Delta E}\_{\text{PFAS}} represents the average binding energy across four representative PFAS compounds (PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, and PFHxS), and Δ​E¯Interf\overline{\Delta E}\_{\text{Interf}} denotes the average binding energy for interferent species (humic acid and SDS), as illustrated in Figure [S14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F14 "Figure S14 ‣ E.2.2 Selectivity Scoring for PFAS Sensor Performance ‣ E.2 A/B Dueling Prompt ( DR Report A vs. DR Report B ) ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery"). A larger positive Δ​Δ​E\Delta\Delta E value indicates superior selectivity, signifying stronger preferential binding to PFAS over interferents. #### E.4.2 Battery Binder Adhesion Performance

The mechanical integrity of lithium-ion battery cathodes critically depends on binder adhesion strength, particularly under the chemically aggressive conditions of liquid electrolyte environments. To evaluate candidate binder materials proposed by the DR agents (Figure [S31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F31 "Figure S31 ‣ E.4.2 Battery Binder Adhesion Performance ‣ E.4 Battery Binder ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")), we employed the same computational framework described for PFAS sensors, with binding energies normalized by the interfacial contact area AA to account for varying polymer–cathode interaction footprints. The contact area was determined through convex hull analysis of atoms within 3.5 Å of the NCM811 surface, enabling direct comparison of adhesion strength per unit interfacial area. Static DFT calculations reveal favorable adhesion for all candidates, with areal-normalized binding energies ranging from 0.0150.015 to 0.1110.111 eV/Å2 (Figure [S32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F32 "Figure S32 ‣ E.4.2 Battery Binder Adhesion Performance ‣ E.4 Battery Binder ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). These values, equivalent to 0.24–1.78 J/m2, align well with established benchmarks for dry interface adhesion, such as graphene on SiO2 (∼\sim0.45 J/m2) and metal–oxide contacts (∼\sim2 J/m2). Candidates B4 and B1 demonstrate the strongest adhesion, while the benchmark PVDF falls in the mid-range, suggesting potential improvements over current commercial binders. However, the introduction of explicit battery electrolyte (EC:EMC:LiPF6 = 9:9:2:2 at 1.25 g/cm3) through AIMD simulations dramatically alters the adhesion landscape (Figures [S33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F33 "Figure S33 ‣ E.4.2 Battery Binder Adhesion Performance ‣ E.4 Battery Binder ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery") and [S34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F34 "Figure S34 ‣ E.4.2 Battery Binder Adhesion Performance ‣ E.4 Battery Binder ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")). Following the same protocol of 2 ps equilibration and 3 ps production runs, most candidates exhibit negative Δ​EpotES/A\Delta E\_{\text{pot}}^{\text{ES}}/A values, indicating that the separated, electrolyte-wetted interface becomes energetically favorable over the bound state. This solvent-induced adhesion reversal reflects competitive adsorption of electrolyte molecules at the binder–cathode interface, disrupting direct polymer–surface interactions. Four exceptions stand out in this trend: candidates A3 (sulfonyl–polyimide), B2 (lignin + CNT), C1 (PVA), and C2 (CMC + WBPU) maintain positive Δ​EpotES/A\Delta E\_{\text{pot}}^{\text{ES}}/A even in explicit electrolyte, indicating robust wet adhesion despite first-layer solvent and ion crowding. Mechanistically, S-PI (A3) presents dense imide carbonyl and sulfone dipoles that support Li+-bridged, multidentate contacts while its aromatic backbone provides broad dispersive π\pi contact; the lignin+CNT composite (B2) couples phenolic/ether O donors (ion–dipole/H-bonding) with a large-area CNT π\pi interface that helps offset solvent-displacement penalties; PVA (C1) contributes a high density of hydroxyl groups enabling multidentate H-bonding and Li+-mediated coordination to surface sites with sufficient chain flexibility to maintain conformal contact; and the CMC+WBPU hybrid (C2) combines inner-sphere/ion-paired adhesion from CMC carboxylates (O⋯\cdotsLi/TM) with urethane H-bonding and local solvent exclusion by the WBPU soft segments. The performance scoring normalized to the PVDF baseline (Figures [S35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#A5.F35 "Figure S35 ‣ E.4.2 Battery Binder Adhesion Performance ‣ E.4 Battery Binder ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery") and [6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2511.18303v1#footnote6 "footnote 6 ‣ Figure S36 ‣ E.4.2 Battery Binder Adhesion Performance ‣ E.4 Battery Binder ‣ Appendix E LLM-as-Judge Rubric and Templates ‣ Hierarchical Deep Research with Local–Web RAG: Toward Automated System-Level Materials Discovery")) quantifies this wet-interface reordering: candidates optimized for dry adhesion may underperform under operating electrolyte conditions, whereas others show unexpected compatibility. These results underscore the need for explicit-solvent, potential-controlled calculations in binder screening, since interfacial energetics in liquid electrolytes are governed by solvent layering, ion crowding, and potential-dependent desolvation that vacuum or implicit-solvent models cannot capture.
